read.sections.0.heading.source: Schools are deciding how to use AI
read.sections.0.heading.back: Schools are deciding how to use AI

read.sections.0.text.source: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use them? In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had any guidance about these tools. Later that year, UNESCO wrote guidance for governments. It asked them to protect students' privacy and to set a minimum age, such as 13, for children talking with these chat tools on their own. This is advice, not a law. Each country and school makes its own rules.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and write whole essays. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use them? In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations body for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had any guidance about these tools. Later that year, UNESCO wrote guidance for governments. The guidance asked governments to protect students' privacy and set a minimum age, for example 13, for children who chat with these tools on their own. This is advice, not a law. Each country and school makes its own rules.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Nigeria: an AI tutor with teachers in the room
read.sections.1.heading.back: Nigeria: an AI tutor with teachers in the room

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2024, World Bank researchers tested an AI tutor in nine state schools in Benin City, Nigeria. The students were in their first year of senior secondary school, usually about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came to computer rooms after school, twice a week, to practise English with an AI chat tool. Teachers trained for the project started each session with a first question to ask the tool. Then they walked around, helping students stay on task. At the end, these students did better on an English test than similar students who were not chosen. The researchers say the result came from the whole programme, the tool and the teachers together.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2024, World Bank researchers tested an AI tutor in nine government schools in Benin City, Nigeria. The students were in their first year of upper secondary school, usually about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came to computer rooms after school, twice a week, to practise English with an AI chat tool. Teachers trained for the programme started each session with a first question to ask the tool. Then they walked around the room, helping students stay focused on the task. At the end, these students got better results on an English test than similar students who were not chosen. The researchers say the result came from the whole programme, the tool and the teachers together.
read.sections.1.text.note: "state schools" is "sekolah kerajaan" (government schools), the Malaysian term; "project" is "program", never "projek".

read.sections.2.heading.source: Türkiye: practice with a tool is not the same as learning
read.sections.2.heading.back: Türkiye: practising with a tool is not the same as learning

read.sections.2.text.source: In 2023, researchers worked with nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at a high school in Türkiye. In four maths lessons, a teacher reviewed a topic, students did practice problems, and then they took a test with no books or computers. During practice, some students had only their books. Some had a chat tool that could give full answers. Others had a tutor version that gave hints, using answers and common mistakes written by their teachers. Both AI groups did much better in practice. But on the test alone, the full-answer group did worse than the books-only group. The tool had become a shortcut. The hint group did about as well as the books-only group. Each study was one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may differ.
read.sections.2.text.back: In 2023, researchers worked with nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at a secondary school in Türkiye. In four maths lessons, a teacher reviewed a topic, students did practice questions, and then they sat a test without books or computers. During practice, some students had only their books. Some had a chat tool that could give full answers. Others had a tutor version that gave hints, using answers and common mistakes written by their teachers. Both AI groups did much better in practice. But on the test without help, the full-answer group did worse than the group with only books. The tool had become a shortcut. The hint group got about the same results as the group with only books. Each study was only about one subject in one place, so results in other places may differ.
read.sections.2.text.note: "on the test alone" is "dalam ujian tanpa bantuan" (on the test without help).

On the test alone, the full-answer group did worse. The tool was a shortcut. The hint group did about the same as the books group. Each study was one subject in one place.

watch.summary.source: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It is a bit like sending messages to a person. The video explains what chatbots are and how they work. It also asks why many of them are made to sound like people. A chatbot can sound friendly and human. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they are. But a chatbot is not a person. It does not really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice how a chatbot makes you feel. And check what it says before you trust it.
watch.summary.back: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It is a little like sending messages to someone. This video explains what a chatbot is and how it works. This video also asks why many chatbots are made to sound like humans. A chatbot can sound friendly and like a human. This can make it feel like a friend. This can also make its answers feel truer than they really are. But a chatbot is not a human. It does not really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice your feelings while using a chatbot. And check what it says before you believe it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Don't ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for schoolwork, and don't ask them to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks governments to set an age limit for children's independent conversations with generative AI tools; its press release names 13, and news reports said some argue for 16. It is advice to governments, not a law or a rule for every learning tool, and many learners are younger than 13. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline.

educatorNotes.1.source: The two studies, simplified (claims/DW11.md). Nigeria (De Simone and others, World Bank, 2025): a randomised trial in nine public schools in Benin City, Edo State, June to July 2024, with first-year senior secondary students (typically 15). Students chosen at random could attend twelve 90-minute after-school sessions (at most two a week) using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4). Teachers had three days' training, began each session with a prompt, guided students without teaching directly and circulated to keep them on task; monitors supervised the sessions. On a pen-and-paper test at the end, gains were 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 on English, with better end-of-year exams too. The authors say the whole programme, tool and teacher guidance together, drove the result; they can't separate the AI's part from the teacher guidance, and don't know how long it lasts or whether it works in other subjects. Türkiye (Bastani and others, PNAS 2025; design from the 2024 working paper): nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at one large high school, autumn 2023; four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of the year's maths; the AI was available only during practice, with a teacher present. With GPT-4 in practice, grades rose 48% (plain chat tool) and 127% (hint tutor built with teachers' solutions and common mistakes); on the closed-book test afterwards, the plain-tool group scored 17% lower than the books-only group, and the tutor group about the same. Neither study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
educatorNotes.1.back: The two studies, briefly (claims/DW11.md). Nigeria (De Simone and colleagues, World Bank, 2025): a randomised trial in nine public schools in Benin City, Edo State, June to July 2024, with first-year upper secondary students (usually 15). Students chosen at random could attend twelve 90-minute after-school sessions (at most twice a week) using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4). Teachers received three days' training, began each session with a prompt, guided students without teaching directly and moved around the room to keep students focused on the task; monitors supervised the sessions. On a pen-and-paper test at the end, the gain was 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 for English, with better end-of-year exam results too. The authors say the whole programme, tool and teacher guidance together, produced the result; they cannot separate the AI's role from the teacher guidance, and don't know how long the effect lasts or whether it works in other subjects. Türkiye (Bastani and colleagues, PNAS 2025; design from the 2024 working paper): nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at one large secondary school, autumn 2023; four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of the year's maths; the AI was available only during practice, with a teacher present. With GPT-4 in practice, marks rose 48% (plain chat tool) and 127% (hint tutor built with teachers' solutions and common mistakes); on the closed-book test afterwards, the plain-tool group scored 17% lower than the books-only group, and the tutor group about the same. Neither study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
